growth_story.headline: Cameroon's income per person collapsed after 1986, and three decades of slow recovery have brought it back only to where it stood in 1981.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Cameroon peaked in 1986, at the end of a boom built on oil and farm exports, and then fell for years as prices for oil, coffee and cocoa dropped, oil output shrank and the real exchange rate rose. From 1990 to 1997 it shrank by 3.7 percent a year on average; the sources date the turn to the January 1994 devaluation of the CFA franc, and the data show growth turning positive from 1995. Since 1998 income per person has grown by 1.1 percent a year, a period the sources link to structural reforms, with debt relief completed in 2006. Growth then slowed from 1.1 percent a year in 2006–2015 to 0.5 percent in 2016–2025, as oil output kept falling, conflicts hit the Far North and the North-West and South-West, and the pandemic cut income per person by 2.4 percent in 2020. Income per person is now 19.2 percent below its 1986 peak, about where it first was in 1981.

threads.text: From the mid-1980s, falling prices for oil, coffee and cocoa sharply worsened what Cameroon earned for its exports. Oil output declined and the real exchange rate rose, and income per person fell every year from 1987 to 1994.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a stable economy with steady overall growth since the mid-1990s, but income per person grew only 0.5 percent a year over 2016–2025 and is still 19.2 percent below its 1986 peak. Most of that overall growth has only kept pace with a growing population. The sources also place the recovery's start at the 1994 devaluation, while the data's era break comes in 1998, because the weak years just after 1994 sit inside the 1990–1997 era.
